selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: config_020 is the simplest configuration available, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA-2000 encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later results can be measured against. 3. Why it is the best next run: PCA-2000 is the RNA encoder with the most direct one-factor partners in the list. These include the scVI and scGPT single-profile RNA models (encoder effect), the multiprofile avgpool and transformer RNA models (profile and aggregation effects), and the PCA-based single-profile multimodal models (effect of adding images, and concat versus weighted fusion). Starting from this baseline means each later experiment can change one factor at a time and still be interpreted cleanly. It also avoids assuming early on that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will do better.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_020) reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, and most remaining configurations are multimodal or image-based. 2. What this tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model is the simplest image counterpart to the RNA baseline. Comparing the two in the same single-profile setting shows how much signal the images carry on their own. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: This one result guides a large share of the remaining search. If images are weak, the search should focus on RNA encoders and profile or aggregation choices. If images are competitive, fusion and multiprofile combinations become worth testing. It is a cleaner first step than jumping to a multimodal model, where a gain or loss could not be attributed to either modality.

1) Evidence so far: there are only two single-profile results. RNA-only with PCA reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Image-only with ResNet50 reached only 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. So RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far. 2) What this tests: config_030 keeps RNA-only and the PCA encoder fixed and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps on its own, without fusion or a transformer aggregator confounding the result. 3) Why it is the best next step: most of the remaining search space is multiprofile, so the answer narrows that whole branch. A gain would justify exploring multiprofile aggregation and fusion next. No gain would point the search back toward single-profile setups and RNA encoder comparisons. Adding the weak image modality now would be less informative.

1) Evidence: RNA is far stronger than image. RNA PCA single-profile reached 0.485 accuracy, while ResNet50 image-only reached 0.208. Switching RNA PCA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy to 0.591 (F1 0.573), so multiprofile avgpool with PCA is the best setting so far. We still do not know whether adding image features helps, does nothing, or hurts in this best setting. 2) config_019 keeps config_030 fixed (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_030 isolates the marginal value of the image modality, using the same image encoder already tested alone. 3) Whether to go multimodal is the decision that shapes most of the remaining search space, since most untested configs are multimodal. A single-change test of it from the current best gives the most information per experiment. If image adds nothing, we can focus the budget on RNA encoders and aggregation (e.g. config_010, config_003, config_045). If it helps, fusion type and image encoder become worth exploring.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool clearly helped RNA, raising accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591. Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion gave a further small gain, to 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. ResNet50 image-only performance was very weak (0.208), so the image representation is a key open question: the image branch may be adding little because the encoder is poor. 2. Test: config_037 keeps everything from the current best (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of image representation in the strongest setup. 3. Why now: It is a one-variable change from the best configuration, so it works as both exploitation and a clean ablation. A gain would show that a better image encoder raises the value of multimodal fusion and point later experiments toward ViT-based variants. No gain would suggest the image modality adds little regardless of encoder, shifting the budget toward RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion choices.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile with avgpool is the largest gain so far. For RNA-only PCA it improved validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591. Adding image features gave a smaller gain: 0.619 with ResNet50 and 0.629 with ViT-L, though ViT-L had slightly lower F1 (0.599 vs 0.610). Profile aggregation is therefore the strongest lever found, but only avgpool has been tested. Transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and the non-PCA RNA encoders are all untested. 2) Test: config_047 differs from the current best (config_037) only in aggregation, transformer instead of avgpool. This isolates whether learned aggregation over profiles adds value beyond mean pooling. 3) Why now: This is a one-variable change on the best configuration, so the result can be attributed to aggregation. It also builds directly on the strongest signal so far. If the transformer helps, it becomes the new base for later fusion and RNA-encoder tests. If it does not, we can fix avgpool and spend the remaining budget on RNA encoders and fusion.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile clearly helps RNA (0.485 to 0.591). Adding images gives a modest further gain (0.619 with ResNet50, 0.629 with ViT-L). Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.599 vs 0.629). Fusion is the one design axis never tested: every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_018 is identical to the current best, config_037 (pca_n2000, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool), except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. Changing only this one choice isolates the fusion effect. Weighted fusion may also let the model lean on the stronger RNA signal and down-weight the weak image modality. 3. Value: This answers an open design question with a clean single-variable comparison. It is also a reasonable exploitation step, since it extends the best configuration found so far. RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT) remain an important next axis to test afterward.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool clearly beats singleprofile for RNA (0.591 vs 0.485). Adding images gives a smaller gain (up to 0.635), and imagenet_vit_l slightly beats resnet50. The transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool, and weighted fusion edged out concat (0.635 vs 0.629, also higher F1). The best result so far is config_018 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted). RNA appears to be the dominant modality, yet every experiment so far has used pca_n2000. The RNA encoder is therefore the largest untested design choice. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps the best setup fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scgpt. Comparing it with config_018 isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: The encoder of the dominant modality probably has the largest remaining effect on accuracy. Testing it inside the current best configuration both explores an uncharted dimension and could directly improve the top result.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.635, F1 0.618). Swapping only the RNA encoder to scGPT (config_009) dropped accuracy sharply to 0.542, so the RNA encoder looks like the most influential choice. The other changes (fusion type, image encoder, aggregation) moved accuracy by only about 0.01–0.03. scVI-200 is the one RNA encoder that has never been tested. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the RNA encoder to scVI-200. It cleanly tests whether a compact learned representation can match or beat PCA, or whether PCA's advantage holds across learned encoders. 3. It closes the largest remaining gap on a high-impact design choice with a single-variable comparison. It is also a plausible candidate for a new best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_034 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. That is well above the matched PCA run, config_018 (0.635). Images alone look weak: single-profile ResNet scored 0.21. Fusion and image-encoder changes have shifted results by only about 0.01–0.03. So the big gain appears to come from the RNA representation, but it is unclear how much of config_034's score depends on the image modality at all. 2) This test: config_045 runs scVI RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool. Comparing it with config_030 (PCA RNA-only, multiprofile avgpool, 0.591) isolates the scVI effect without images. Comparing it with config_034 isolates the image contribution once RNA is strong. 3) Why now: if scVI RNA-only nearly matches config_034, the multimodal complexity adds little and the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices. If it falls well short, fusion with images is confirmed as valuable, and later tests of concat versus weighted fusion and transformer aggregation with scVI are justified. One run answers a core design question that fine-tuning near config_034 would not.

1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter. 2. config_051 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is a hub configuration. It gives a starting reference point and has untested neighbours that each differ by exactly one design choice: aggregation (config_049, avgpool), fusion (config_037, concat), RNA encoder (config_028 scVI, config_043 PCA), image encoder (config_001, ResNet50), modality (config_022 RNA-only, config_005 image-only) and profile setting (config_014, single-profile). 3. Under a limited budget, anchoring on this hub lets each later experiment isolate the effect of one choice. That is more informative than starting from an isolated configuration. The choice of hub is not an assumption that the most complex model will win; the unimodal and single-profile ablations are planned to test exactly that.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; config_051) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. We do not yet know how much each modality contributes. 2. What this tests: config_022 keeps the same RNA encoder (scGPT), multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation, but drops the image branch. Only the modality setting changes, so the comparison isolates what the ViT-L image features add on top of scGPT. 3. Why now: whether multimodality helps at all is the highest-level design choice. Its answer shapes how the rest of the budget is spent: refining fusion and image encoders if the image branch helps, or focusing on RNA encoders, profile setting and aggregation if it does not. Settling it first is more informative than tuning secondary choices around a single anchor result.

1) Evidence: Multimodal scGPT+ViT-L (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. RNA-only scGPT with the same multiprofile and transformer setup reached 0.514 accuracy and a higher 0.498 F1. This small, mixed difference leaves open whether the image modality carries useful signal or adds little beyond RNA. 2) This experiment: Image-only ViT-L with the same multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation completes the modality comparison while holding profile setting and aggregation fixed. It shows directly how much predictive signal the image representation provides on its own. 3) Why now: If image-only performs poorly, the remaining budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation or profile choices rather than fusion variants. If it performs well, fusion design (weighted vs concat) and image encoder choice deserve further exploration. Settling this modality question first is the most efficient way to guide the many remaining multimodal options.

1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal so far. RNA-only scGPT with transformer reached 0.514 accuracy and the best F1 (0.498). Image-only ViT-L scored only 0.260. Adding the image to scGPT gave a negligible accuracy gain (0.520) and a lower F1 (0.479), so how much the image helps is still unclear. The largest untested factor is the RNA encoder: only scGPT has been tried. 2) This experiment keeps everything the same as config_022 (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and swaps scGPT for PCA (n=2000). That isolates the effect of the RNA representation and checks whether a pretrained foundation model actually beats a simple linear baseline. 3) Under a limited budget this is the best next step. RNA dominates performance, so the RNA encoder choice will shape every later multimodal and aggregation comparison. A clean single-factor test on the cheap RNA-only branch resolves this before spending experiments on fusion or image-encoder variants. If PCA matches or beats scGPT, the search should be redirected.

1. Evidence so far: all four completed runs use the multiprofile setting with transformer aggregation. RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only models with scGPT (0.514 acc / 0.498 F1) and PCA (0.519 acc / 0.480 F1) are nearly tied. Adding ViT-L image features to scGPT gives only a marginal accuracy gain (0.520) and lowers F1. Image-only is weak (0.26). The main untested design choice is the profile setting: we do not yet know whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all compared with single-profile modeling. 2. What this tests: config_012 is the single-profile counterpart of config_022 (RNA-only, scGPT). It changes only the profile setting, giving a clean estimate of what multiprofile modeling contributes. 3. Why this is the best next run: the comparison costs little and isolates one variable, and its answer sets the direction for the rest of the budget. If single-profile matches or beats multiprofile, the search should shift toward simpler single-profile configurations. If it clearly underperforms, multiprofile is confirmed and later runs can focus on aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) and RNA encoder choice.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for scGPT RNA-only (0.514 vs 0.411 accuracy). The two RNA encoders performed about the same (scGPT 0.514, PCA 0.519). Adding ViT-L images with weighted fusion gave no clear gain (0.520), consistent with image-only being weak (0.260). Every multiprofile run so far used transformer aggregation, so we do not know whether the transformer actually drives the multiprofile gain. 2. What this tests: config_006 keeps the strong scGPT RNA-only multiprofile setup (config_022) fixed and changes only aggregation, from transformer to avgpool. This is a clean single-variable test of aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next step: aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, including all multimodal ones. Settling it in the simplest strong baseline will tell us how to prune or prioritize much of the remaining search space. It is more informative than another multimodal variant, where image gains so far look marginal.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT with avgpool (0.530 acc, 0.515 F1). With transformer aggregation, that same RNA-only setup reached 0.514. Adding ViT-L images with weighted fusion under transformer aggregation gave 0.520, only slightly higher. Image-only models are weak (0.26), so it is still unclear whether the image modality adds anything. 2. This experiment tests multimodal scGPT + ViT-L with avgpool and weighted fusion. It differs from the current best (config_006) only by adding the image modality. It also differs from config_051 only in aggregation. So it gives a clean check of whether images help on top of the strongest RNA setup, and whether the avgpool advantage holds in the multimodal setting. 3. It exploits the most promising direction (multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) while settling the main open design question, whether multimodality is worth it, with a single-variable comparison. That makes it the most informative use of the next run.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.542). Avgpool has beaten transformer aggregation in both the RNA-only pair (0.530 vs 0.514) and the multimodal pair (0.542 vs 0.520). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (scGPT RNA-only: 0.411 vs 0.514–0.530). Fusion is the one design axis never tested, since every multimodal run used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_038 changes only weighted to concat fusion on the best configuration. This isolates the fusion effect directly. It also shows whether a different fusion scheme makes better use of the weak image signal (image-only 0.26). That matters because multimodal's gain over RNA-only is small, and its F1 (0.483) is lower than RNA-only avgpool (0.515). 3) Value: This is a one-variable comparison anchored on the current best. It answers an untested design question while exploiting the strongest region found so far, so it is informative whether concat helps or hurts.

1. Evidence: Avgpool has beaten transformer aggregation twice: RNA-only scGPT (0.530 vs 0.514) and multimodal weighted (0.542 vs 0.520). The current best is config_049 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion). Under transformer aggregation, PCA_n2000 roughly matched scGPT in RNA-only (0.519 vs 0.514). So the RNA encoder choice is still unresolved, and scGPT may not be needed. 2. Test: config_045 keeps everything from config_049 and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000. This isolates whether the foundation-model RNA representation helps in the best-performing setting, or whether a simpler PCA representation does as well or better. 3. Why now: It is a single-variable change to the current best configuration, so it exploits the strongest direction while also answering a key representation question. Image-only results are weak (0.26), so changing the image encoder is likely less informative than the RNA encoder, which drives most of the performance.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_045 (PCA RNA + ViT-L image, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. That is well above every other run. With scGPT, multimodal gave only a modest gain over RNA-only (0.542 vs 0.530 under avgpool). Under transformer aggregation, PCA and scGPT performed about the same in RNA-only (0.519 vs 0.514). The missing control is RNA-only PCA with avgpool. Without it, we cannot tell whether config_045's jump comes from PCA plus avgpool alone or from PCA features combining well with image features in fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 changes only one thing from config_045, removing the image modality. It also completes the RNA-only encoder × aggregation grid (PCA vs scGPT, avgpool vs transformer). If config_036 scores near 0.63, the RNA representation and aggregation drive performance. If it stays near 0.52–0.53, the gain comes from PCA-specific multimodal complementarity. 3. Why this is the best next run: The result decides where to spend the remaining budget. Either we exploit the multimodal PCA direction further (image encoder, fusion, transformer variants) or we focus on cheaper RNA-only refinements. It also checks how far config_045's single result can be trusted, before we build on it with less diagnostic exploitation runs.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no reference point for how well any representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice performs. 2. What this tests: config_031 is the simplest configuration in the space. It uses RNA only, a single profile, a PCA (2000-component) encoder, and no aggregation or fusion. Its validation accuracy and F1 set a baseline floor. Later experiments can then each change one factor from this anchor: scVI or scGPT encoders for representation, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer for profile setting and aggregation, image-only for modality, and adding images with concat or weighted fusion. Each change can be attributed to that factor rather than confounded with others. 3. Why this is the best first use of the budget: starting from a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would leave us unable to tell whether any gain comes from images, multiple profiles, the aggregation method or the fusion method. A simple baseline also guards against assuming that complexity helps, and it maximises what every later comparison can tell us.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n2000) baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about how profile setting, modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion affect performance. 2) Question: config_013 keeps the model setting (RNA-only) and RNA encoder (PCA n2000) fixed. It switches only to multiprofile with avgpool, the simplest aggregation. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles improves on the single-profile baseline. 3) Why now: profile setting runs through most of the search space, since most multimodal configurations are multiprofile. Settling it early with a clean one-factor comparison against the existing baseline tells us whether to focus later experiments on multiprofile designs, before we spend budget on more complex aggregation, image or fusion choices.

1) Evidence: with RNA only and PCA features, moving from a single profile (config_031, acc 0.485) to multiple profiles with avgpool (config_013, acc 0.591, F1 0.573) gave a large gain on both metrics, about 0.10. That makes multiprofile avgpool a strong working baseline. The image modality is completely untested, and it is the largest open design question. 2) Test: config_045 keeps everything from config_013 the same (multiprofile, PCA RNA encoder, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to adding images. 3) Why now: whether images help or hurt decides whether the remaining budget goes to the many multimodal configurations or to refining RNA-only encoders and aggregation. This single-variable comparison gives the most information per experiment, while also extending the best-performing setup.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain for PCA RNA-only (0.485 to 0.591). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a smaller gain (0.591 to 0.619, with F1 0.573 to 0.610). We do not know how much signal the image branch carries alone. The modest multimodal gain could mean images are weak, or that images are strong and concat fusion is not using them well. 2. What this tests: config_008 runs image-only with ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool, matching config_045 except that the RNA branch is removed. It completes a clean modality ablation (RNA-only vs image-only vs multimodal) under the same profile and aggregation setting. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The result decides where to spend the remaining budget. If image-only nears or beats multimodal, image encoder and fusion choices deserve priority. If it is weak, RNA encoder choice (scVI or scGPT) and aggregation become the main levers. One run answers this, which is a better use of budget than tuning secondary choices before the basic modality contributions are known.

1. Evidence: Moving RNA (PCA) from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool gave the largest gain so far (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion added only a modest further gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.328). So profile aggregation looks like the most influential design choice, but only the simple avgpool aggregator has been tried. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the current best configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles improves on mean pooling. 3. Value: It builds directly on the best configuration while changing a single factor, so the result is interpretable. Whichever way it turns out, it tells us whether later experiments should use transformer or avgpool. Image-encoder (config_002) and fusion (config_030) swaps are the natural next one-factor comparisons, but aggregation is the design axis with the strongest evidence of large effects.

1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.328. Adding images to the PCA multiprofile model gave a modest gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). Multiprofile clearly beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485), and avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). The RNA encoder is the main untested choice: every run so far used pca_n2000, so we do not know whether scVI or scGPT embeddings would do better. 2) Test: config_025 keeps the current best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation on the dominant modality. 3) Why now: because RNA dominates performance, its representation is likely the most consequential remaining choice. A single-variable change from the current best is both exploitative, since it could beat 0.619, and informative, since it starts mapping the encoder axis. It is a better use of budget than testing the image encoder or fusion type, which affect the weaker modality or a smaller design detail.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool beats singleprofile (0.591 vs 0.485 RNA-only with PCA). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). Adding images helps modestly (0.591 to 0.619 with PCA). Swapping PCA for scVI gives the current best, config_025 at 0.632 accuracy, though its F1 is similar to PCA's. ResNet50 image features are weak on their own (0.328 image-only), and the alternative image encoder, imagenet_vit_l, has never been tested. So the image representation is a large untested design choice that may be limiting how much the image modality contributes. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the image encoder relative to the best configuration (ResNet50 to ViT-L, keeping scVI, multiprofile, avgpool and concat). Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image representation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it resolves the most consequential unexplored dimension with a single-variable comparison. It is also a logical extension of the strongest configuration, so it has good odds of improving the best result. Weighted fusion and scGPT can be tested afterwards on whichever image backbone wins.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Switching the image encoder from resnet50 to ViT-L gave about +8 points. Changing the RNA encoder from pca to scvi gave only a small, mixed gain (+1.3 accuracy, slightly lower F1). Multiprofile with avgpool beats singleprofile and transformer aggregation. scGPT has never been tested, so it is the largest open question among the RNA encoders. What this tests: config_034 changes only the RNA encoder (scvi_n200 to scGPT) within the best setup, isolating whether a foundation-model RNA representation adds value once the strong ViT image features are present. Why now: it explores a completely untested design level in the context most likely to perform well. Either outcome is informative: a gain would set a new best, and no gain would let us fix the RNA encoder and focus remaining budget on fusion (weighted) and ablations such as image-only ViT.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Several design choices already have some evidence. Multiprofile beat singleprofile for PCA RNA (0.591 vs 0.485). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.619 vs 0.579). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L improved results substantially with scVI (0.632 to 0.715). scGPT performed poorly (0.518). Fusion, however, is completely unexplored: every multimodal run has used concat. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy within the strongest region of the search space. 3. Why now: Fusion is the one major design axis with no evidence at all, so this experiment reduces the most uncertainty. Because it is a single change from the current best, it is also a plausible route to a further gain, so it balances exploration and exploitation better than other options.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy. Swapping only the image encoder from ResNet50 (config_025) to ViT-L raised accuracy from 0.632 to 0.715, the largest single-factor gain observed. The only image-only baseline uses ResNet50 (config_008, 0.328). So we do not know how much signal ViT-L carries alone, or whether the multimodal model's advantage comes mostly from the image side. Fusion type (concat vs weighted, 0.715 vs 0.706) and avgpool vs transformer aggregation look secondary, and scGPT appears weak. 2. Test: config_012 (image-only ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool) differs from config_008 only in the image encoder, giving a clean unimodal measure of ViT-L. Compared with config_004, it also shows how much RNA adds on top of the stronger image encoder. 3. Why now: This resolves a key uncertainty, whether the gain reflects true multimodal complementarity or simply a much better image representation. That guides whether remaining budget should go to RNA and fusion refinements or to image-side choices, at the cost of one experiment.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no reference point for whether RNA, image, multiprofile aggregation or fusion adds value. 2. Test: this runs the simplest configuration, an RNA-only, single-profile model on a PCA (2000-component) encoder. It sets a baseline that later changes can be compared against one factor at a time. PCA has direct neighbours in the pool: the multiprofile avgpool and transformer versions (config_041, config_015), and multimodal single-profile pairings with each image encoder (config_012, config_029, config_028, config_040). Using these, RNA-encoder comparisons with scVI (config_010) and scGPT (config_014) can follow. 3. Value: under a limited budget, an inexpensive and interpretable anchor is the best first experiment. It avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and it makes every later experiment easier to interpret.

1. Evidence: only one result exists, an RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. That gives no information yet on which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_041 keeps the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (PCA-2000) fixed and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile. It uses the simplest aggregation, avgpool, so any difference can be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to a learned aggregator. 3. Why now: the profile setting runs through most of the remaining search space, so knowing early whether multiprofile helps tells us whether to prioritize multiprofile configurations. A clean one-variable comparison against the existing baseline is the most informative use of the next experiment. Adding image data or changing the encoder would remain open for later isolated tests.

1) Evidence: with the PCA RNA encoder held fixed, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose similarly (0.464 to 0.573). This is fairly strong early evidence for the multiprofile setting. The biggest open question is whether the image modality adds anything, since no image-containing configuration has been tested yet. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup unchanged (PCA RNA, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. It therefore isolates the marginal value of adding images to the best RNA-only model. 3) It builds directly on the strongest result while answering the most important design question: whether going multimodal is worth exploring further. 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at about 0.65 accuracy versus about 0.51-0.52 for scGPT and PCA. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin (0.650 vs 0.520). Avgpool and transformer aggregation perform almost identically (0.650 vs 0.653). The one multimodal run, scVI + ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion, scored 0.632. Weighted fusion could let the model down-weight a weaker or noisier image signal rather than diluting the strong scVI representation. 3) Why now: the main open question is whether multimodality adds value over the strong RNA-only baseline. A single-variable fusion comparison on the best-known backbone answers it directly. It also has a realistic chance of becoming the new best configuration. If weighted fusion also fails to beat RNA-only, that points next to testing image quality, such as image-only or ViT-L runs, rather than spending budget on further fusion variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.678, F1 0.646). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal multiprofile scVI + ViT-L with avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion (config_045: 0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L (config_024 to config_045) and concat for weighted fusion (config_022 to config_024) each improved results. scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA, and multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. The main gap is that no image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell how much of the multimodal gain comes from the image features versus genuine fusion with RNA. 2) Test: config_046 is image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool. If image-only comes close to 0.706, effort should shift to image-side choices. If it falls well short, refining fusion and aggregation in the multimodal setup (for example config_034) is justified. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_045 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, and multiprofile beats singleprofile. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.715 accuracy). 1. The best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy. It clearly beats RNA-only scVI (about 0.65) and the ResNet50 multimodal variant (0.63). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Test: config_049 keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting the same and adds image features (ImageNet ViT-L) through simple concat fusion. Evidence: in the single-profile setting with PCA RNA features, adding ImageNet ViT-L image features via concat fusion raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.535, and F1 rose in parallel. That gain has two possible explanations. Image features may complement RNA, or images alone may be the stronger signal, with RNA adding little or even diluting it. This experiment tests the image-only single-profile ViT-L model, which completes the modality comparison under identical profile and encoder settings. It will show whether the multimodal gain reflects true fusion benefit or mostly image signal. That answer shapes the rest of the search: either keep investing in fusion and RNA encoder choices, or prioritize image-centric and multiprofile image settings. Under a limited budget, one cheap baseline that removes the main ambiguity in the existing result is worth more than jumping to more complex multiprofile configurations, which would change several factors at once.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal single-profile PCA plus ViT-L with concat fusion (acc 0.535, F1 0.519). It beats RNA-only (0.485), and image-only is weak (0.227). This suggests RNA carries most of the signal and imaging adds some, but each setting has only one run. Profile setting has not been tested at all, and it is a major design axis. 2) Test: config_027 keeps the best configuration's RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion. It switches only to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), which multiprofile requires. This gives a near-clean test of whether multiprofile inputs help over single-profile. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the strongest result while answering a large open question. If it helps, transformer aggregation (config_022) is the natural follow-up. If it does not, the budget can move to RNA encoder or fusion comparisons within the single-profile setting.

1. Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.535 (config_049) to 0.629 (config_027), with F1 rising similarly. Multimodal concat also beat RNA-only (0.485), and image-only was weak (0.227). The strongest signal so far is that multiprofile aggregation matters, but only one aggregation method (avgpool) has been tried. 2. Test: config_022 keeps everything from the current best fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Why now: This extends the most promising direction while varying a single factor, so any change can be attributed to aggregation alone. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality, with RNA-only at 0.485 versus image-only at 0.227. Adding images helps modestly (0.535 vs 0.485 single-profile). Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. scVI clearly beat PCA (0.629) and scGPT (0.518) under the same setup. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Moving from avgpool to transformer aggregation gave a clear gain of about 0.056, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.03. But the only image-only run (ResNet50, avgpool) was weak at 0.33, and no RNA-only model has used transformer aggregation or scVI. So it is unclear how much of the top score comes from the image modality versus RNA with transformer aggregation. 2) This experiment is an RNA-only ablation of the best pipeline: scVI, multiprofile, transformer, with the image branch removed. If it scores near 0.72, fusion adds little. If it scores much lower, the image branch genuinely contributes. It also shows whether the transformer gain holds without images. 3) Small fusion tweaks (concat vs weighted differed by about 0.004) or exploitative variants carry little information. This single-factor ablation resolves a central design question, whether multimodality is necessary, before more budget is spent refining fusion or image encoders.
